content.title: About
content.content: Bread with onion is a traditional baked product in which finely chopped onion rings or onion powder are mixed into the dough. The loaf has a fragrant, slightly sweet onion flavor and a crisp crust. It is often enjoyed as a snack, a side for soups, or as a base for sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Onion bread is popular in Eastern European and Mediterranean cuisines.
Adding onion to dough increases moisture and extends shelf life thanks to onion’s natural antimicrobial properties.
In some regions the bread is baked as round rolls, while elsewhere it appears as long loaves.
The onion enhances aroma, allowing the bread to be served without additional seasonings.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Onion provides quercetin and sulfides that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports immune system
items.content: Vitamins C and B6 found in onion contribute to immune function.

items.title: May lower cholesterol
items.content: Onion sulfides have been shown to help reduce LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Bread supplies fiber, and the added onion contributes additional dietary fiber.

items.title: Onion allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to onion.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Onion can cause increased gas and digestive discomfort in sensitive people.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is used in the recipe, watch overall sodium intake, especially for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy bread with onion as a standalone snack, serve it alongside soups, use it for sandwiches, or cut it into cubes for salads. A warm slice pairs well with butter or cream cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bread in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag and reheat in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Monterey reduced‑fat cheese is a semi‑hard cheese with a mild flavor, made from low‑fat cow’s milk. It has a bright orange rind, a light texture, and less fat than traditional Monterey Jack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Monterey cheese originated in California in the early 20th century and is named after the city of Monterey.
The reduced‑fat version was developed in the 1990s to lower calories while keeping the taste.
It is frequently used in Mexican cuisine: tacos, burritos, and fajitas.
The cheese melts easily, making it popular for casseroles and sauces.
The orange color comes from natural coloring agents such as paprika or annatto.

items.title: Lower fat content
items.content: Reduced fat makes it more suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Like most cheeses, it provides calcium that supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Contains complete milk protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic cultures
items.content: Fermentation creates beneficial bacteria that can aid gut microbiota.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains lactose, so people with intolerance should limit consumption.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to casein.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The cheese can be salty; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite reduced fat, it remains calorie‑dense; portions should be moderate.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Monterey reduced‑fat cheese works well sliced in sandwiches, grated over salads, in casseroles, sauces, and Mexican dishes. It melts quickly in the oven or on a skillet and can be used as a filling for burritos.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. Once opened, keep for about 2‑3 weeks. Discard if mold appears or the cheese develops an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee creamer powder, flavored (406) is a dry substitute for liquid cream designed to enhance the taste and texture of coffee. The powder dissolves quickly in hot or cold beverages, giving them a creamy smoothness and the selected flavor (vanilla, caramel, hazelnut, etc.).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Powdered creamer is easier to store and transport than liquid cream.
Flavorings can be natural or artificial depending on the formulation.
The fat content is usually lower than in traditional cream, making it more suitable for diet drinks.
It is widely used in commercial coffee shops to ensure consistent flavor across large volumes.
A broad range of flavors is available: vanilla, caramel, hazelnut, chocolate, spice blends.

items.title: Improved flavor
items.content: Flavored powder adds a smoother, sweeter taste to coffee, reducing the need for added sugar.

items.title: Convenient usage
items.content: Easy to dose, requires no refrigeration and retains its properties for a long time.

items.title: Lower calorie option
items.content: Compared with whole cream, the powder often contains fewer calories and less fat.

items.title: Texture enhancement
items.content: Creates a creamy foam and improves the mouthfeel of the drink.

items.title: Stable storage
items.content: Does not spoil quickly and does not need cold storage.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Some formulas contain dry milk, which can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Artificial flavorings
items.content: Synthetic flavors may cause sensitivity in susceptible consumers.

items.title: Additive overload
items.content: Certain versions may include stabilizers and emulsifiers that should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 1‑2 teaspoons of powder to hot or cold coffee and stir until fully dissolved. Increase the dose for a richer taste. The powder also works well in lattes, cappuccinos, dessert drinks, and cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. When stored properly, the shelf life is 12‑18 months. After opening, close the package tightly to prevent moisture absorption.

egg-sandwich-on-croissant-with-ham.title: Egg sandwich on croissant with ham

content.title: About
content.content: An egg sandwich on a croissant with ham is a buttery, flaky croissant split open and filled with a soft boiled egg, slices of ham, and often a touch of cheese or fresh herbs. The combination of layered pastry, rich croissant flavor, and protein‑rich filling makes it a popular breakfast or light snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Croissants originated in Austria but are now a hallmark of French pastry.
The egg‑and‑ham sandwich has been a staple in European cafés for over a century.
Ham used in the sandwich is typically cured pork shoulder, lightly smoked for added aroma.
Butter‑rich croissant dough contains more calories than regular bread because of its high fat content.
Some cafés top the sandwich with avocado or tomato for extra freshness.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs and ham provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Both ham and egg contain vitamin B12, important for nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Eggs and meat offer heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Egg yolk is rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, antioxidants that protect the eyes from age‑related decline.

items.title: Provides sustained energy
items.content: The croissant supplies quick carbs while the protein and fat slow absorption, keeping you fuller longer.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A butter‑laden croissant with ham can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Processed ham often contains a lot of salt, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Individuals with egg allergy should avoid this sandwich.

items.title: Trans fats in pastry
items.content: Some commercial croissants may contain partially hydrogenated oils; choose varieties without trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich warm, freshly reheated in an oven or toaster. It pairs well with leafy greens, mustard, mayo, or sliced avocado for added flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. The croissant may lose crispness; reheat in the oven for 5‑7 minutes before serving to restore its flaky crust.

rice-white-with-carrots-and-tomatoes-and.title: White Rice with Carrots and Tomatoes

content.title: About
content.content: White rice cooked with carrots and tomatoes (or a tomato‑based sauce) is a nutritious dish popular in many world cuisines. Rice provides energy, carrots add sweetness and vitamin A, and tomatoes contribute lycopene and vitamin C.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The rice‑carrot combination is traditional in Asian and Mediterranean recipes.
Tomatoes increase iron absorption from rice thanks to their vitamin C content.
White rice has a higher glycemic index than whole‑grain varieties, so it is often paired with vegetables to slow sugar release.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Tomato sauce can be made from fresh tomatoes, olive oil, and herbs, adding aroma to the dish.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice is a primary source of carbohydrates, delivering quick energy.

items.title: Vitamin A from carrots
items.content: Beta‑carotene supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene is a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes are high in vitamin C, which boosts immunity and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The dish contains virtually no fat unless oil is added, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or tomato products.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying carrots and tomatoes, choose organic or wash them thoroughly to reduce pesticide exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice with carrots and tomatoes as a side dish or a main course. Add herbs (parsley, basil), a drizzle of olive oil, or a splash of lemon juice for extra flavor. The dish reheats well in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it can be kept for up to 2 months after cooling completely.
